The type of tibial component can significantly impact mechanical alignment in unicompartmental knee replacement (UKR). Specifically, patients who received a metal-backed Onlay tibial component tend to have better postoperative mechanical alignment compared to those who received all-polyethylene Inlay prostheses. The thicker overall construct of the Onlay prostheses is thought to be an important determinant of postoperative alignment.

Studies have shown that different types of tibial components can lead to varying levels of mechanical dysfunction and instability, which can impact the success of UKR. For example, a study found that patients who received metal-backed Onlay components had improved postoperative alignment compared to those who received all-polyethylene Inlays. This suggests that the type of component may play a role in determining the level of mechanical stability achieved after UKR.

However, it's essential to note that other factors also contribute to mechanical alignment, such as patellar positioning and ligament balancing. The gaps in patella eversion demonstrated smaller gaps both in knee extension and flexion position compared to the gaps of patella reduction position. These findings suggest that intraoperative patellar positioning is an important consideration during gap balancing.

In conclusion, while the type of tibial component may contribute to mechanical alignment in unicompartmental knee replacement, it is just one factor among many that can impact the success of this surgical procedure. Further research is needed to fully understand the relationship between component type and mechanical alignment, as well as other factors that may influence the outcome of UKR.
